title: Parliament passes national gas reservation scheme before summer break
excerpt: Gas exporters will have to offer part of their supply to Australian buyers first under a scheme that cleared federal parliament on Friday.
content_html:
Federal parliament on Friday passed laws creating Australia's first national gas reservation scheme, which will require major exporters to make part of their supply available to local buyers before it is shipped overseas.

The House of Representatives sat briefly on Friday morning to agree to changes the Senate made to the bill late on Thursday, the last scheduled sitting day of the year.

What the scheme does

Under the scheme, large gas producers must offer Australian buyers up to 20 per cent of the volume they plan to export. The rules also aim to keep supply about 10 per cent above expected domestic demand, so the local market has a buffer.

The obligation is due to start on 1 January 2028, NCA NewsWire reported. Gas contracts signed before the government announced the policy in December 2025 will be honoured, according to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.

Western Australia, which has run its own reservation policy since 2006, has been carved out so its existing arrangements can continue. The exemption followed lobbying by the WA government and the Coalition.

Government and opposition

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the law would put downward pressure on what households and businesses pay for gas. "This is a proud moment for our government," he told reporters in Canberra.

Resources Minister Madeleine King said the change would shift bargaining power towards buyers such as manufacturers and energy companies when they negotiate long-term contracts. Asked for modelling on how much bills would fall, Albanese did not give a figure or a date.

The Coalition said it would not block the bill, after securing the Western Australian carve-out. The Coalition had raised concerns during debate about how the scheme would treat that state.

The Greens argued the scheme does not go far enough. Greens senator David Shoebridge dismissed it as an empty gesture and renewed his party's push for a tax of at least 25 per cent on gas exports, which he said would do more to lower prices. "This is the gas reservation bill that the gas industry wants," he said on Thursday.

Industry concerns

Producers raised objections while the bill was before parliament. At a Senate inquiry, Shell executives warned the 10 per cent oversupply target was excessive and could lead to market failure, AAP reported. The government had earlier changed the 20 per cent figure from a minimum to a maximum after industry feedback, and producers can fall short of the target with government approval.

End of the parliamentary year

The gas scheme was the last of four priority bills Labor wanted passed before parliament rises for summer. Earlier in the week, parliament also passed online safety laws, changes to private health insurance rebates for people over 65, and a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts. Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has said a Coalition government would repeal the trusts tax.

Parliament is due to return in early February.
